title: The Crusades
summary: The Crusades were military campaigns organised by popes and western Christian powers to take Jerusalem and the Holy Land from Muslim rule and then hold them. After the Byzantine emperor Alexios I asked for help against the Seljuks, Pope Urban II called the First Crusade at Clermont in November 1095. Crusaders took Jerusalem in 1099 and founded the Crusader States. Saladin won at Hattin in 1187, the Fourth Crusade turned on Constantinople in 1204, and Acre, the last stronghold, fell to the Mamluks in 1291.

uncertainty.note: Spanning from Pope Urban II's council at Clermont in 1095 to the fall of the last major mainland crusader stronghold at Acre in 1291; later regional crusading efforts continued in the Baltic, Iberia, and eastern Europe.

importance.justification: Two centuries of war over the Levant between Latin Christians and Muslim powers; its parts have their own records (R3 D3 T3 L2).

audience_note: Describes religious warfare, sieges, military violence, and the massacre of civilian populations during the capture of Jerusalem and sack of Constantinople.

related.because: The First Crusade march across Europe and Asia Minor captured Jerusalem in 1099 and established the crusader states.
The five-week siege and bloody storming of Jerusalem in July 1099 achieved the initial expedition's goal.
Saladin's victory at the Horns of Hattin crushed the field army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, prompting the Third Crusade.
The Fourth Crusade was diverted to Constantinople, looting the Byzantine capital and partitioning the empire.
The siege and fall of Acre in 1291 eliminated the final Latin crusader foothold on the Levantine coast.
